description: Our name, Spectrum 21, is inspired by the 21-centimeter hydrogen line that astronomers use to map the distant cosmos. We are a team focused on transforming  datasets and scientific theories into  tools by leveraging our skills in software engineering, data analysis, design, and scientific research.
summary: We created Curators of Silence: The Museum of Off-World Heritage as an interactive educational museum game set in 2126 .It allows young explorers to investigate historic spacecraft, inspect real hardware, and uncover what NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. It meets the challenge by turning complex mission histories  into a story based experience for ages 7 to12 and takes it a step further: players explore a 3D Mars and Moon archive, collect clues from real spacecraft parts, test engineering systems, and build their own museum exhibits. What makes it matter is that it is not just a static space facts page; it is a hands on detective museum. We used authentic NASA mission records and NSSDCA resources across missions like Spirit, Sojourner, Phoenix, Apollo 11, and LRO to bring silent hardware back to life. It doesn't just show a list of which machines were left behind, but reveals why they stopped and what they discovered, making the science behind exploration unforgettable.
details:
What does it do?


Most websites about old space missions are long technical articles filled with dates and jargon. Young students rarely feel connected to the silent rovers, landers, and stages still resting on the Moon and Mars. Curators of Silence solves this by turning space history into an interactive mystery web game set in a virtual museum in the year 2126. Players become trainee curators who investigate real NASA machines Spirit, Sojourner, Phoenix, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module, and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).

 

How does it work?

Player start in a rotating 3D archive centered on Mars with a portal to the Moon. Anyone who prefers a simpler view can also explore through the Mission Archive list or the 2D Ghost Map.Each playable case has six simple steps:

  1. Mission Briefing: Read the mission story and learn the mystery question.
  2. Machine Inspection: Click 6 real hardware parts to collect evidence clues.
  3. Engineering Lab: Explore systems like power, heat control, movement, communication, and science tools, then answer a quick check question.
  4. Evidence Wall & Timeline: Review your collected clues with NASA source links and put  mission events into the right order.
  5. Solve the Mystery: Use your clues to answer the main case question and a short science follow-up.
  6. Create an Exhibit: Choose a photo, pick three discoveries, write a short reflection, and save or print your own museum card.

We also built The Wider Archive, which shares cards and NSSDCA/NASA links for the rest of the historic spacecraft from the challenge list including the Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP packages, Surveyor, Viking 1 and 2, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and Kepler.

Figure 1: The 3D Mars and Moon Archive homepage

 

What benefits does it have?

  • Curators of Silence delivers immediate value by running straight in any web browser with no logins, accounts, or downloads. Clues, scores, and saved exhibits stay stored locally, making it easy for students, parents, and teachers to jump right in.
  • The platform empowers all kinds of learners to explore comfortably offering a rotating 3D archive on desktops alongside tap controls, keyboard support, a flat Mission Archive list, and a 2D Ghost Map for phones, tablets, and school computers.
  • Instead of overwhelming 7–12-year-olds with dense technical articles, short visual cards, engineering checks, and timeline puzzles help young players see how spacecraft design directly leads to real scientific discoveries.

Figure 2 : Machine Inspection of Spirit, players click hardware hotspots to collect clues and learn why each engineering part mattered

 

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Kids usually hear only about active missions, while older landers stay hidden in technical archives. Our goal is to help young space fans feel a personal connection to these silent explorers.

By showing how a machine was engineered (like Apollo 11 leaving its Descent Stage behind to save fuel for liftoff, or Spirit getting stuck before the dark Martian winter) alongside what it discovered, players gain a real understanding of space engineering and how past missions paved the way for today's exploration.

Figure3: The Engineering Lab and Timeline Reconstruction of PHOENIX

 

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did you use?

  • Coding Languages: JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SVG (for technical diagrams, icons, and the 2D Ghost Map), using browser localStorage to save player progress.
  • Frameworks & Libraries: React, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber (for the interactive 3D Mars and Moon scene).
  • Hosting & Version Control: Deployed on Vercel and managed with GitHub.
  • Design & Media Tools: Custom museum-style SVG diagrams and authentic NASA and ESA photos, textures, and 3D resources .
  • Hardware: Laptop and mobile devices for building and testing both 3D controls and touch layouts.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Instead of building a standard encyclopedia, we placed the learner in the year 2126 as a heritage curator solving cases.
  • Each case ends with Create an Exhibit, turning students from passive readers into museum curators who write and design their own display card.
  • Including LRO as "The Orbital Witness" shows how an active lunar orbiter photographed the Apollo 11 equipment still sitting at Tranquility Base decades later.

Figure 4: The Ghost Map of Moon, players explore real landing sites across Mars and the Moon to see where NASA's historic spacecraft still rest and jump straight into each mission's story

 

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • We Built this for School Age Explorers ages 7–12. We kept paragraphs short, used clear color cues like gold for actions, cyan for science notes, green for completed clues, and avoided confusing jargon where simple words worked better.
  • Every interaction works by click, tap, or keyboard rather than hover alone. We also included simple move buttons for timeline puzzles and a flat Mission Archive view for anyone on a phone, tablet, or basic school computer.
  • Because our audience includes young students, we saved clues, scores, and exhibits directly in the browser so players never need an account, password or personal details.
  • We verified facts against NASA and NSSDCA records, placed source links right beside images, and clearly separated our fictional 2126 museum setup from real mission history.

Figure 5: The Wider Archive introduces more silent explorers like Viking, Ingenuity, Dawn, and Pioneer with direct links to their real resting places and official NASA NSSDCA records

 

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

We used Super Intelligence (AI) tools (Gemini  and Claude) in a supporting role while building this project specifically for brainstorming ideas, improving grammar and sentence flow for our final submission, and helping debug our code. We did not use any AI-generated images, audio, or video. All mission photos and planetary textures come from official NASA and partner archives, and all technical facts were checked against NASA mission records.
